# Idle Master

> A small Windows utility that frees 1.5-2 GB of RAM by closing the background
> updaters, launcher services and tray webviews nobody opened on purpose, then
> keeps them from respawning. Services are stopped, never disabled, so a reboot
> undoes everything.

- Platform: Windows 10 and 11, x64. Free to use, source available.
- License: FSL-1.1-MIT. Free for any use including commercial and internal
  business use; the only prohibited use is selling a competing product or
  service built on it. Each release converts to the MIT license two years after
  publication. Copyright 2026 Mild-Solvent.
- Download: https://github.com/Mild-Solvent/Iddle-Master/releases/latest/download/IdleMasterSetup.exe
- Source: https://github.com/Mild-Solvent/Iddle-Master
- Site: https://mild-solvent.github.io/Iddle-Master/
- Documentation: https://mild-solvent.github.io/Iddle-Master/docs.html — the full
  manual: install, the two modes, the sentry, every idlemaster.ini setting with
  its default, the command line, recovery steps.

## What it does

Two modes:

- **BOOST NOW** frees roughly 1.5-2 GB and leaves your session intact. It closes
  updaters, launcher services, tray webviews and the search indexer. Anything you
  opened yourself survives, and any process whose window is on screen is skipped.
- **ABSOLUTE IDLE** is for a machine nobody is sitting at. It also closes
  browsers and chat apps, and recycles the Windows shell, landing the machine near
  1.5-2 GB in use total - the Windows kernel and Defender floor.

**Restore desktop** puts back exactly what the last run took away.

## Why it is different from other RAM cleaners

Most memory optimizers free memory once and the software respawns within the
hour. Idle Master runs a **sentry**: a background thread that re-applies the same
kill lists every 20 seconds, re-stops services every 5 minutes, and trims working
sets every 10 minutes. The RAM stays freed instead of drifting back up.

It does not claim to "compress" or "defragment" memory. The mechanism is closing
processes that should not have been running, and keeping them closed.

## Measured results

On a real machine with 15.9 GB total and 11.4 GB in use:

| Software | RAM | Closed by |
|---|---|---|
| Brave, 28 processes | 5.0 GB | absolute idle |
| Claude desktop, 17 processes | 3.0 GB | absolute idle |
| VPN client UI, service and updater | 760 MB | boost + idle |
| msedgewebview2, 17 tray and widget hosts | 540 MB | boost |
| Windows shell (explorer, search host), recycled | 490 MB | absolute idle |
| Razer Cortex, Central and services | 305 MB | boost |
| NVIDIA overlay and ShadowPlay | 110 MB | boost |
| Lenovo Vantage and add-ins | 90 MB | boost |
| Windows Search indexer | 60 MB | boost |

`IdleMaster.exe --report` prints this table for the reader's own machine and
changes nothing.

## Safety design

- **Protected list wins.** `[protect]` and `[protect.services]` are checked before
  any kill, even if the same name is on a kill list.
- **Remote access is guarded.** Whatever the user reaches the machine with - RDP,
  Parsec, Moonlight, Sunshine, SSH, a mesh VPN like Tailscale - goes in
  `[protect.services]`. Before finishing, and repeatedly in idle mode, the tool
  verifies the service is running, a port is listening and the adapter is up, and
  restarts it if it died. The machine cannot lock the user out.
- **The connection itself is guarded.** A standing **network guard** checks every
  minute, whenever the app runs, that a network link is up, the internet answers,
  Tailscale is running with an address, and Sunshine is listening - and repairs
  the first thing that is wrong with an escalating ladder: restarts WLAN/DHCP/DNS
  services, turns the Wi-Fi radio and auto-connect back on, reconnects Wi-Fi to a
  known network (a preferred list, then every saved profile; it never scans or
  asks for location unless NetworkGuardScan=1), renews DHCP,
  flushes DNS, bounces the adapter, restarts Tailscale or runs `tailscale up`,
  restarts Sunshine. It never drops a link Tailscale is still up through, backs
  off after six failed tries, and can also stop Windows powering the Wi-Fi
  adapter down. `--network` runs one check from a script; `--guard` runs only the
  guard from the tray.
- **Ping is not proof.** If ICMP to the anycast addresses answers while TCP to
  both of them fails, the guard calls that trouble in its own right: on a
  stranded machine the router still pings, because it is a directly connected
  route, and nothing else works.
- **It clears what a stopped VPN leaves behind.** A VPN client stopped after
  being connected can leave its adapter up holding 0.0.0.0/1 and 128.0.0.0/1
  pointed at a dead gateway, plus DNS servers that only ever resolved through
  the tunnel. Between them those two routes cover the whole address space and
  are more specific than the real default route, so the machine looks online and
  nothing connects. The guard removes both halves and that DNS - every step
  gated on no service of that VPN running, so a live tunnel is never touched.
- **Nothing is disabled.** Services are stopped only, so a reboot restores the
  machine with no further action.
- **Every run is recorded** and can be undone with `--restore`.
- **It asks first.** Anything started after the mode ran gets a prompt showing the
  app's icon and description, with Keep it / Always keep / Trash once / Always
  trash. No answer within 47 seconds means "trash once" by default (configurable).
- **Open windows are never touched** in boost mode, including an app's background
  worker processes, resolved by walking the parent chain.
- **`[protect.tree]` spares an app and every helper underneath it**, resolved the
  same way. It exists for the WebView2 and Electron family: WhatsApp and Discord
  do their real work in child processes named `msedgewebview2`, which is on the
  boost list. Sparing the parent alone leaves a tray icon receiving nothing.
- **Respawn backoff.** If one process returns 6 times, the sentry stops fighting it
  for 30 minutes rather than burning CPU in a kill loop.

Absolute idle terminates `explorer.exe` and Winlogon rebuilds the session on its
own: the desktop, taskbar and Start menu come back within seconds, fresh and a few
hundred MB lighter. The screen flashes black, and open File Explorer windows do
not survive it. The whole shell family - explorer, sihost, StartMenuExperienceHost,
ShellExperienceHost, ShellHost, SearchHost, TextInputHost - is protected in code,
so no sweep can hunt the rebuild. If the rebuild never arrives, the recovery is
Ctrl+Shift+Esc, File, Run new task, IdleMaster.exe, Restore desktop - Task Manager
is hosted by winlogon so it works with no shell running. Setting `KillExplorer=0`
disables this behaviour.

## Backup kit

The **Backup kit** window writes one zip for reinstalling Windows: the installed
apps you tick (reinstalled through winget, one at a time), the files and folders
you tick (copied back where they were, old profile path remapped to the new
account), Idle Master with your idlemaster.ini, and optionally two well-known
scripts run on the new machine - zoicware/RemoveWindowsAI (Copilot, Recall,
non-interactive) and Chris Titus WinUtil (a preset applied headless, then left
open). The zip contains IdleMasterRebuild.exe, a plain-text rebuild.ini,
apps.json in winget-import format, and files\. Building a kit changes nothing.

## Disk cleanup

A separate window, unrelated to RAM. It reads the drive's own file table and
lists what it found: temp files, caches, crash dumps, Windows update leftovers,
old installers, the recycle bin, possible leftovers from uninstalled software,
and big folders. Every finding opens into what is actually inside it, with an
owner column naming the app the bytes belong to and a safe-or-review verdict.
The same scan can be shown as a folder tree or as a treemap of the whole drive.

Nothing is deleted until the user ticks something and presses Clean, and what is
ticked goes to the **Recycle Bin** - with one exception the confirmation names
out loud: `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download` is deleted outright,
because moving hundreds of thousands of files to the bin takes hours and frees
nothing until the bin is emptied. `[cleanup.protect]` is never touched at all.
Each item names itself and its size before it starts, and Stop cleaning prevents
the next item starting. `--cleanup-report` prints the findings and deletes
nothing.

## Debloat

Removes preinstalled Store apps: it lists every removable package with its
category (preinstalled junk, sponsored apps, Xbox and gaming, Microsoft extras,
everything else), its package name and its size, and removes only what is
ticked. This is an uninstall, not a boost - no reboot brings it back and the
only undo is the Store, which is why the Store itself, winget, the App
Installer, Windows Terminal, WSL, the app runtimes, the codec extensions and the
NVIDIA display stack are protected in code where no config edit can reach them.
`[debloat.protect]` adds the user's own. `--debloat-report` lists and removes
nothing.

## Remote desktop setup

Adds the user's own apps to the network guard's watch. `[remote.apps]` is the
list; **Calibrate now** records each app's exe, its service and the ports it is
listening on while everything is connected the way the user wants it, and from
then on every check restarts or relaunches anything that no longer matches that
picture.

## Reporting a bug

A **Report a bug** button writes a report containing the build, the Windows
version, whether it was elevated, and the last lines of idlemaster.log, shows it
byte for byte in a preview, and then opens github.com with it pre-typed. Nothing
leaves the machine until the user presses Submit in their own browser.

## Themes

Idle Master ships three looks inside the exe: Minimalistic (the default, and the
look the app has always had), Terminal (green phosphor on black) and Cortex
(rounded, gradient-lit, with a title bar the theme draws instead of Windows).
The picker appears once, on first run, over a blurred copy of the running
window; after that it is Settings > Theme.

A theme is a plain text file - nineteen colours, two font families and six keys
for shape - saved as themes\name.imtheme next to the exe. No plugin, no DLL, no
code in a theme. All three built-ins are written out on first start so the way
to make a fourth is copy, edit, restart. Switching is instant and does not need
a restart; only a change of window frame waits for the next start.

Extra themes are deliberately NOT bundled in the installer, to keep the download
small: "Get more themes" fetches IdleMasterThemes.zip from the same GitHub
release the app updates itself from and unpacks the .imtheme files locally.

## Install and use

The app checks GitHub for a newer release every 6 hours (UpdateCheckHours) and
offers a one-click in-place update from a tray toast or the main window; the
config file is never touched by an update.

Installing needs no administrator; the app elevates itself at runtime because
stopping services requires it. Install path is
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\IdleMaster`. The config file `idlemaster.ini` is never
overwritten by an update.

```
IdleMaster.exe               open the window
IdleMaster.exe --boost       boost mode, no UI
IdleMaster.exe --idle        absolute idle, no UI
IdleMaster.exe --restore     undo, and stop the sentry
IdleMaster.exe --report      print what is eating RAM, change nothing
IdleMaster.exe --cleanup-report  scan the disk, print findings, delete nothing
IdleMaster.exe --debloat-report  list removable Store apps, remove nothing
IdleMaster.exe --boost --watch   boost, then keep hunting
IdleMaster.exe --unwatch     stop the sentry
IdleMaster.exe --network      check link, internet, Tailscale, Sunshine; fix what is down
IdleMaster.exe --guard       run only the network guard, in the tray
IdleMaster.exe --installtask run the sentry (and the guard) at every logon
IdleMaster.exe --installtask --guard   only the network guard at logon
IdleMaster.exe --removetask  undo that
```

Builds with the .NET Framework compiler already present in Windows:
`powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File build.ps1`. No SDK, no NuGet, no
internet access required.
